A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RISE research work. All 20 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v2, including their appendices, support comparison; equations, tables, figures, and relocated material could be matched.

before.justification: V1 reports original mathematical benchmark results, component ablations, error analyses, sensitivity experiments, and generated-solution case studies.

after.justification: V2 retains original mathematical experiments and adds logical-reasoning and code-generation results, additional model comparisons, and robustness experiments.

M1.justification: The central sampling, step editing, edit-distance filtering, and DPO/NLL objectives remain unchanged. Appendices F–G add an unrestricted-error editing variant that removes predefined error-type instructions and is also used for code generation, constituting a limited procedural adaptation.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates mathematical reasoning only. V2 adds ZebraLogic logical reasoning, MBPP and HumanEval code generation, and training on medium/hard LeetCode problems. The six original mathematical evaluation datasets remain; the larger GSM8K/MATH training experiment changes sampling within existing coverage.

E2.justification: The comparator membership in the original main comparisons is retained. V2 Tables 8–9 add Ministral-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, together with their DPO variants, as comparators against corresponding RISE models on GSM8K/MATH. Standard DPO itself was already evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce Puzzle/Cell Accuracy and code pass@1 evaluation, a 15K-problem mathematical training pool, additional model configurations, and code training with 50 sampling attempts. Separately, v1 explicitly reports tool-assisted ToRA/MAmmoTH results, whereas v2 states that results use the same CoT prompts and omits that exception. This revises the reported protocol without establishing that those baselines were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds tests of training-data choice, four edit-distance thresholds, self-instruct prompt templates, and unrestricted-error prompts in Appendices D–F. Section 3.5 also examines transfer from mathematical training to other reasoning tasks. The original component ablations, error analysis, sampling/pair-count studies, error-mixture study, and case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The manual error-detection audit remains 46 correct classifications among 50 checked samples. Additional candidate-solution sampling in v2 is not repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results for transfer, code training, additional models, and robustness settings in Tables 4 and 8–14. It also revises RISE-Llama-3.1-70B scores, including MATH from 66.1 to 66.4 and Odyssey-MATH from 58.9 to 60.0. The new code-training comparison reports RISE at 44.2/47.6 versus DPO at 43.4/46.3 on MBPP/HumanEval; these are distinct from the mathematical-training transfer results.

T1.justification: The underlying edit-distance filter, step/full-solution DPO definitions, and adaptive NLL objective in Equations 1–3 are retained. V2 compresses mathematical notation but adds no substantive derivation, formal assumption, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: V1's central effectiveness claims concern mathematical reasoning. V2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion explicitly extend the contribution to transferring mathematical preferences into logical reasoning and code generation, broadening the claimed capability to general reasoning. The core error-injection and training-stabilization claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning prompt flexibility, coverage of arbitrary errors, and reduced generalization with overly permissive edit-distance thresholds. A new Limitations section identifies untested knowledge-based reasoning in law, medicine, and finance. Existing explanations of AIME failure and possible harm on complex mathematical tasks remain.

D1.justification: V2 supplies additional prompt templates, preparation counts for new experiments, and a LeetCode dataset access reference, while retaining the original software versions and training hyperparameters. V1's Section 6 statement that all code and data are supplied in supplementary material disappears without a replacement; this establishes a disclosure change, not verified withdrawal of resources.

R1.justification: The introduction reframes prior step-wise methods around inter-step consistency and contrasts this with RISE's inner-step errors. V2 adds Xu et al.'s SRA-MCTS citation and removes the ORPO and Common 7B Language Models citations. Its two Setlur entries describe the same previously cited work, rather than two distinct additions.

P1.justification: Rewriting is concentrated in the abstract and introduction, with explicit contribution bullets and new inner-step/inter-step terminology. The main section sequence and most method and retained experimental prose remain similar. New analyses shift appendix numbering, while the original case studies and prompt set remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 substantially redesigns the document from one-column to predominantly two-column layout, shrinking and relocating retained displays and stacking the formerly side-by-side ablation tables. It adds result and prompt tables plus an introductory pie-chart presentation of the error breakdown. Existing framework diagrams and sensitivity plots are retained rather than replaced by new analyses.

improvement.justification: The added prompt and hyperparameter checks address previously untested design dependencies, while transfer and code-training experiments broaden validation. These benefits outweigh limited reporting deterioration, but the gain is constrained by removal of the code/data availability statement and inaccuracies in new interpretations: Section 3.5 claims a 2.8-point Qwen2 Cell Accuracy gain, whereas Table 4 shows 21.5 to 23.2, a 1.7-point gain.
